articleTitle: ASTRA Broadband Interactive System-a Ka-band return path for IP connectivity
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Multimedia Services and Digital Television by Satellite (Ref. No. 1999/111)
abstract: The ASTRA Broadband Interactive System provides a Ka-band return path transmitted from a satellite interactive terminal located at the user premises thus complementing new and existing ASTRA Ku-band forward path services by forming a 2-way end-end network via satellite. The forward path is DVB/MPEG-2 based offering data rates of up to 38 Mbit/s and the return path utilises multiple frequency time division multiple access (MF-TDMA) to efficiently allocate bandwidth on-demand at data rates of up to 2 Mbit/s from a 120 cm antenna. The ASTRA Broadband Interactive System will utilise the Ka-band payload on ASTRA 1H, which has been launched in June 1999, and will become the first pan-European Ka-band commercial service. The commercial launch is planned for mid 2000.

articleTitle: Towards the convergence of interactive television and WWW
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Multimedia Services and Digital Television by Satellite (Ref. No. 1999/111)
abstract: Watching the television has traditionally been a passive activity, where broadcasters provide a selection of programs and the viewer chooses a single program from that selection. In the past there was only a single television set in each house and viewing was often a family activity. The falling cost of sets coupled with greater affluence has led to an increase in the number of television sets within a household. One result of this has been a tendency to make viewing a more solitary occupation. Television has had to compete with other forms of home entertainment, notably personal computers and games consoles. The former offers access to the Internet as well as providing games, while the latter not only provides an alternative to viewing broadcast television, but may also use the TV set as its output device. With the arrival of digital broadcasting has also come the possibility of interactive television. Already, a number of countries have either introduced, or are currently in the process of introducing interactive services. These services are often similar to those available via the Internet and for some time it has been suggested that these are converging technologies. We look at the history of both interactive television and World Wide Web (WWW) technologies, draw a parallel between them and show how convergence is already taking place. Finally a number of possible models for future convergence are presented.

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Multimedia Services and Digital Television by Satellite (Ref. No. 1999/111)
abstract: Although satellite data services have been available for quite some time, the costs associated had restricted their adoption to corporate customers with very specific needs. However, factors like the surge in demand for Internet connectivity and the development of low-cost DVB receivers have re-activated the interest in providing data services over satellite. As a result, a number of competitors have (or will shortly) entered the IP over satellite market offering differently packaged services. BT Satellite Systems have been involved in the development of ways to provide IP services over satellite networks and have investigated a number of technologies (ATM, DVB, ...) and network architectures (bi-directional satellite links, one-way satellite link plus terrestrial return, ...). This paper reviews the work carried out by Satellite Systems to date and explores the new business opportunities offered by the use of DVB platforms.

articleTitle: Development of future multimedia services. BT's Satellite Fast Packet Demonstration Network
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Multimedia Services and Digital Television by Satellite (Ref. No. 1999/111)
abstract: Over the last decade the commercial role of satellite systems has changed, from been a provider of intercontinental circuits in the core network to now being an access technology. Influencing factors in this change of direction have been the vast roll out of fibre optic networks across the world and the associated improvements in SDH reliability and redundancy for international circuits. Commercial applications and requirements for satellite services have also changed from limited narrow-band voice and data to interactive multimedia services. Hence the requirement for the development of a new wave of satellite systems supporting broadband access technologies (IP, ATM and DVB) with defined ground segment interfaces to ensure full integration with terrestrial networks running advanced service management and intelligent agent platforms. To this extent, BT Satellite Systems have developed a Satellite Fast Packet Demonstration Network to raise the profile of satellite systems within the business community.

articleTitle: Can open architectures propel satellite data broadcasting into the mainstream
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Multimedia Services and Digital Television by Satellite (Ref. No. 1999/111)
abstract: Satellite data broadcasting has to date been a niche market, meeting the requirements of the financial world, paging networks, and other information service providers offering high value low speed data feeds. The explosive traffic demands of the Internet industry, and the potential from evolving uses for multimedia, promise massive growth in the use of satellite broadcasting for wide area data distribution. Overviewed are factors representing the 'technology push', such as high power direct to home satellites, mass produced chipsets for multimedia DVB receivers, sophisticated head end multiplexing and off the shelf broadcast aware software applications. Taking this technology out of the confines of demonstrator networks, and into successful commercial deployment, poses new challenges for satellite service providers, and finding corresponding 'market pull' is proving more difficult than market forecasters and industry pundits have foreseen. How can this technology be made reliable and deliverable into large network communities spread across continents? How can system design side step the high costs traditionally associated with satellite, and allow charging structures to encourage take up? How closely can satellite broadcasting emulate familiar data networks, and break down the perception of 'rocket-science'?.

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Multimedia Services and Digital Television by Satellite (Ref. No. 1999/111)
abstract: Open Interactive was created by its shareholders, BSkyB, BT, HSBC and MEI to deliver interactive television. That is, interactivity which is entertaining, informative and easy to use-just like television. Of course that implies that the service will be rich, offering shopping, banking, information services, games and e-mail under the brand name Open. However interactivity as envisaged by Open implies much more than merely displaying Web pages on television, imposing technical requirements on a number of key components of the system, principally the digital set top box and a delivery mechanism which mixes high bandwidth digital satellite transmission with on-line data delivered by the telephone network.
